source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) prompt design, full text (gap 1)
finding: The RPD prompt repeats the default prompt, names the RPD model, and tells the model to match the case to a typical case, simulate the decision, and modify it if it fails. The data-frame prompt lists seven reasoning steps. Both add an Analysis or Reflection field before the answer. No length-matched neutral prompt and no ablation of recall vs simulate was run.
numbers: No word or token counts reported for any prompt. Authors say the effect may partly reflect the additional reasoning process. Odds ratio vs default: RPD 2.26 (z=8.69), data-frame 2.05 (z=7.23).
limits: Single study, ChatGPT models only, one task. No replication found. Gap note: Gap 1 stays open: nothing separates RPD content from extra reasoning text, and which half (recall or simulate) works is unknown.
agent_relevance: Run our own 4-arm test: neutral reasoning of equal length, recall-only, simulate-only, both.

source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) accuracy by urgency category
finding: The overall gain comes almost entirely from the 13 self-care vignettes. Nonemergency accuracy did not move and emergency accuracy fell slightly.
numbers: Overall 63.3% default (CI 61.9-64.7), 67.6% RPD (66.3-69), 66.7% data-frame (65.3-68). Self-care (13 cases): 13.4% to 29.8% RPD, 24.6% data-frame. Nonemergency (30 cases): 82.5 / 82.0 / 82.8%. Emergency (2 cases): 100 / 98 / 99%.
limits: Paper reports accuracy per category, not sensitivity or specificity, so discrimination was not measured directly. Raw error counts absent. Gap note: Gap 9: this looks like a threshold shift toward lower urgency, not better discrimination across the board. Nonemergency flat at about 82% means no gain where most cases sit.
agent_relevance: Do not read this as RPD improves judgement. Track per-class accuracy and the direction of errors, not only the mean.

source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) error direction and stated limits
finding: Across all prompts, 88% of errors were over-triage (higher urgency than needed) and 12% under-triage. In the 2 emergency cases the RPD prompt gave nonemergency advice 2% of the time (CI 0.5-5) and data-frame 1%; the default never did.
numbers: Over-triage 88% (CI 87-88.9), under-triage 12% (11.1-13). Authors: no safety conclusions should be derived. Only 2 emergency cases, 1 benchmark, ChatGPT family only, no human users.
limits: Prompt effects also cost more tokens, as the authors note. Gap note: Gap 9 answered in part: the self-care gain is real on this set, but safety cannot be judged. Prompts that push toward less urgent advice raise accuracy because the default was too cautious.
agent_relevance: A gate on simulation should be tuned to the error cost, not to accuracy alone.

finding: The gain is not universal. GPT-5.2 got no benefit, and gains vary a lot by model. Reasoning models also gained from the RPD prompt.
limits: Ten repeats of the same 45 vignettes, so repeats are not independent cases. Gap note: Gap 1: 8 of 10 models gained with RPD, 2 (GPT-5.2) did not. Data-frame matched or beat RPD overall on 5 of 10 models, so RPD-specific content is not shown to matter.
agent_relevance: Expect scaffold gains to be model dependent; test per backbone.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) re-read: the 80 percent sentence
finding: The 80% figure sits in the section on intuitive decision-making and creativity. It has no in-line citation. It points only to previous empirical research on IDM in sports settings.
numbers: Sentence: expert athletes choose their preferred first option most of the time, in 80% of the decisions made. No sample size, no sport, no reference.
limits: Source of the number remains unknown; treat as unsourced. Gap note: Gap 2: Bossard gives no primary source. The figure is about option choice, not the RPD simple-match rate. Johnson and Raab 2003 is the likely origin but could not be opened, so the link is not verified.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) re-read: Macquet 2020 range and its reference
finding: The 60-81% simple-match sentence is quoted from one book chapter: Macquet (2020), Decision-making in sport: looking at and beyond the recognition-primed decision model, in Human Factors and Ergonomics in Sport, CRC Press, pp. 135-154.
numbers: Sentence: 60-81% of the experts' decisions were classified as intuitive, using simple matching; then 13-28% and 3-24%. No Ns in Bossard. Crossref lists the chapter (doi 10.1201/9781351060073-12) with no abstract.
limits: Cannot name which studies sit at 60 vs 81%. Gap note: Gap 3 stays open: the underlying studies and Ns are not given by Bossard and the chapter is paywalled. The range is pooled from an unnamed set of sport interview studies, so it is second-hand twice over.
agent_relevance: Use the range only as a rough prior that matching dominates, not as a calibrated rate.

source: Del Missier et al. (2014) Option generation in decision making: ideation beyond memory retrieval (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Individual-differences study of option generation in ill-structured scenarios. Fluency was supported by ideation ability beyond memory retrieval. Generating more options raised the quality of the best option but lowered the mean quality of the set.
numbers: Abstract: more options increase the quality of the best option generated but decrease the mean quality of the generated set. Sample N=141 comes from the earlier pass, not re-read here.
limits: Abstract only. Not sport. Does not test choice quality directly. Gap note: Gap 4: this reconciles part of the conflict. More options helps best-of-set but dilutes the average, so whether it helps depends on whether the rater scores the best, the first, or the chosen option.
agent_relevance: Score both best-of-set and first-option quality when testing option count.

source: Klatt et al. (2019) Creative and intuitive decision-making, Brazilian and German coaches and players (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Study 2 (players, real match video): number of options correlated positively with quality of both the first and the final option; the first option was better than later ones; creativity score correlated with first-option quality.
numbers: Two studies (coaches, players), two countries. No Ns in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; sample sizes unread. Correlational across players. Gap note: Gap 4: both findings hold together. First option best on average (take-the-first) and players who generate more options also have better first and final options. This is a correlation across players, not an effect of forcing more options.
agent_relevance: The right design variable is skill-linked option fluency, not an instruction to produce more options.

source: Raab and Laborde (2011) When to blink and when to think (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Handball players who prefer intuition made faster and better choices than deliberative players. Experts were more intuitive than near-experts and non-experts. Authors say the results support take-the-first.
numbers: N=54 handball players of different levels, lab video attack situations. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Lab video task; preference measured, not manipulated. Gap note: Gap 4: supports less-is-more for experts in their own task. Preference is a trait, so causality is not shown.
agent_relevance: Do not force deliberation on a task where recognition already works.

source: Raab and Johnson (2007) Expertise-based differences in search and option-generation strategies (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Two-year longitudinal handball study with eye tracking and verbal protocols. Athletes of all levels generated the same number of options on average, but quality differed by expertise for both initial and final choices.
numbers: Same mean option count across expert, near-expert and non-expert; the difference is in quality. Sample size not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Gap note: Gaps 2 and 4: extends the take-the-first line in handball; the lever is option quality, not count. The founding 2003 paper is still unopened.
agent_relevance: First-option quality is what to improve.

source: Johnson and Raab (2003) Take The First (Org Behav Hum Decis Process)
finding: Could not be opened: the Elsevier landing page returned only a redirect notice. Crossref confirms the record (title, journal, 2003). No numbers obtained.
limits: Paywalled; no open copy found with the tools available. Gap note: Gap 2 remains open: the primary sample and the share of first options chosen could not be verified.

source: Ivanova, Didenko, Grigoryan and Kraevskiy (2025) RPD on financial markets using LLM (Routledge, Decoding AI, pp 98-119)
finding: Crossref confirms a book chapter, 15 Oct 2025, on simulating RPD dynamics in financial markets with an LLM. No abstract on Crossref and the publisher page returned no text.
limits: Not opened; title, venue and date only. Gap note: Gap 5: it is a finance chapter, not sport, and its measures are unknown. Cannot say whether it is a real test of RPD.
agent_relevance: Treat as unverified; do not cite as evidence.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step): CoT can reduce performance where thinking makes humans worse (arXiv 2410.21333), main results
finding: Six psychology tasks where deliberation hurts people were run on LLMs. Reasoning before answering hurt strongly in three: implicit statistical learning, face recognition (language poorly suited to the stimulus) and learning labels with exceptions. In the other three, effects were mixed.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning: GPT-4o direct 87.5% vs CoT 64.4% (-23.1 points); o1-preview vs GPT-4o on a subset -36.3 points; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 (no drop). Random is 50%.
limits: Tasks are classic psychology tasks, not athletic decisions. Gap note: Gap 6: gives a rule for when reasoning-first hurts: stimuli that are perceptual or implicit and hard to put in words. Not a sport study.
agent_relevance: Route perception-like items through a direct answer first.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step: face recognition and exceptions tasks
finding: Verbalising before choosing lowered accuracy on face recognition for all six vision models and slowed learning of labels with exceptions.
numbers: Face recognition (random 20%), direct vs CoT: GPT-4o 64.0 vs 51.2; Claude 3 Opus 44.0 vs 29.6; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 vs 94.8; Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0 vs 54.6. Exceptions task, rounds to learn labels: GPT-4o 2.9 direct vs 12.5 CoT (+331%); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4.
limits: No direct-then-check ordering was tested, so recovery is not shown. Gap note: Gap 6: consistent with SPORTU where rationale-first hurt hard video items (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 52.57% direct vs 39.32%). Drops were smallest for the strongest model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet -3.0 points).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 open on the recovery half: design a direct-then-check arm.

source: Wang et al. (2024) TacticAI: retrieval and refinement results from the full paper
finding: Latent-space corner retrieval was judged usefully similar far more often than a feature-cosine baseline. Player-adjustment suggestions were rated favourable by five Liverpool staff in 45 of 50 cases.
numbers: Retrieval recall 0.63 +/- 0.09 (TacticAI) vs 0.33 +/- 0.10 (feature baseline), 50 pairs, five raters, p<0.05. Refinements: mean rating 0.7 +/- 0.1, 45 of 50 (90%) favourable by majority, t(49)=9.20, p<0.001. Real-vs-generated F1 0.60 +/- 0.04. Raters' receiver top-3 0.79 +/- 0.18.
limits: Five raters, 50 samples, not an LLM, no outcome data. Gap note: Gap 7 stays open: the comparison is against another retrieval method, not against no retrieval, and the outcome is expert opinion, not match results. No controlled outcome trial.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of similar cases is judged useful by experts; the outcome benefit is unmeasured.

source: Individual-sports visual-search meta-analysis (2026, abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Meta-analysis of 26 studies (N=611) in individual sports: experts made fewer fixations, longer fixations and fewer distinct locations than novices.
numbers: Fewer fixations SMD -1.52 (95% CI -2.38 to -0.65); longer fixation duration SMD 0.93 (0.44-1.41); fewer locations SMD -1.27 (-2.26 to -0.28). No moderation by sport type. Risk of bias moderate.
limits: Individual sports only. Abstract only; heterogeneity not read. Gap note: Bears on claim K05: fewer fixations in experts holds pooled in individual sports; the conflict with the team-sport 11v11 result stays a task-dependence story. Authors say visual search is highly task specific.
agent_relevance: Cue selection (fewer, better cues) is the expert signature in constrained tasks.

source: Rugby union decision mechanisms by time available (2021, abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Sixteen semi-elite rugby players in post-game self-confrontation interviews. With more time they used stored declarative knowledge; as time shrank they diagnosed and updated rapidly; sometimes they reported no deliberate process.
numbers: N=16, interviews. No rates in the abstract.
limits: Small N, retrospective speech. Gap note: Gaps 2 and 3: the matching/diagnosing mix moves with time available, so the 60-81% range is time dependent, not a constant.
agent_relevance: Gate deliberation on time or stakes, not on a fixed share.

source: Solopova et al. (2026) LLMs as strategic actors in geopolitical simulations (arXiv 2603.02128)
finding: A search surfaced this as a possible RPD-dynamics paper. It is not one: it never mentions recognition-primed decisions. It compares six LLMs with MBA participants in four crisis simulations.
numbers: Action alignment micro-F1 round 1 (n=63): Gemini 0.540, Claude 0.533, Mistral 0.476, ChatGPT 0.460, Qwen 0.317, Grok 0.254; round 2 (n=45): 0.156-0.333. Krippendorff alpha 0.41 among models.
limits: Negative finding for RPD; not sport. Gap note: Gap 5: rules this paper out as the Ivanova work. Shows LLM alignment with human choices decays across rounds.
agent_relevance: Not evidence for or against RPD.

finding: arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited and the WebSearch budget was spent. Crossref, Europe PMC, direct arXiv PDFs and one PMC page worked. Gap 8 (LLMs on expert-novice text plays) and gap 7 outcome trial found nothing.
numbers: 0 studies found for gap 8; 0 outcome trials for gap 7.
limits: Tool limits. Gap note: Absence is weak evidence.
